Private equity investments in India are generally dominated by growth capital transactions, together with minority and controlled buyouts, structured investments in underperforming companies, and private investments in public equity (“**PIPE****s**”) investments. While investors across sectors have been cautious of the recent geopolitical developments, there has been a steady flow of value-driven investments across sectors. Notably, India witnessed one of its highest quarterly deal volumes, i.e. 710 deals worth USD 16 billion to USD 20 billion in Q1 2026, despite a decline in deal value due to a fall in large transactions. IT/ITES, energy, media and entertainment, banking and financial services, retail and consumer, and healthcare are amongst the top sectors for private equity investments.1 There has also been an increased interest from private equity investors to invest in clean energy and emerging sectors, such as those relating to satellites and launch vehicles.

Regulatory support and continued long-term stability in government policies, tax reforms, and the willingness of the Government to assist and support credible capital source have been some of the key factors encouraging private equity transactions in India.

India continues to pose a favourable environment for investment, owing to strong macroeconomic fundamentals including real GDP growth, moderate levels of inflation and low inflation volatility, a conducive monetary policy, and demographic advantage. Further, India has entered into bilateral trade agreements, thereby enhancing cross-border capital flows through a predictable tariff environment.4

On the other hand, factors such as geopolitical uncertainty have brought about volatility in the supply and cost of energy. Additionally, the depreciation in the Indian Rupee against the USD has resulted in cautious deployment of private capital as it could impact their USD return on capital.

1.3**Are you seeing any types of investors other than traditional private equity firms executing private equity-style transactions in your jurisdiction? If so, please explain which investors, and briefly identify any significant points of difference between the deal terms offered, or approach taken, by this type of investor and that of traditional private equity firms.**

The landscape of foreign investment in India is increasingly diversifying, with investors beyond traditional private equity firms. For instance, sovereign wealth funds and pension funds deploy long-term capital. Family offices participate in growth-stage investments, often offering greater flexibility on deal terms and timelines. Private credit funds and alternative investment funds (“**AIFs**”) pursue hybrid debt equity structures, while hedge funds and domestic conglomerates similarly favour blended financing approaches. One of the key differences in the approach between traditional private equity funds and sovereign wealth funds, family offices and pension funds seems to be their outlook towards exit horizons, as these investors are not pressed to make time bound investments.

In India, private equity transactions are primarily structured keeping in mind the regulatory and tax considerations. Most private equity investments are made through special purpose vehicles that are located in jurisdictions with whom India has a tax treaty. India-based private equity funds also use their funds that are registered with the Indian securities regulator, the Securities and Exchange Board of India (“**SEBI**”), as AIFs to invest in Indian companies. Private equity funds that look to make portfolio investments in Indian listed securities also use their foreign portfolio investment (“**FPI**”) vehicles that are registered with SEBI.

The main drivers of these acquisition structures amongst others are: (i) the nature of the investor; (ii) tax consideration including treaty impact; (iii) the nature of investment, i.e. whether it is a buyout, PIPE deal, on-market portfolio investment etc.; (iv) the nature of the investee entity, i.e. whether it is a listed entity or an unlisted entity; and (v) the exit horizon of the investor.

While making primary investments, investors generally prefer compulsorily convertible instruments, which allow adjustments to the conversion ratio to also take into account performance-linked adjustments as well as any adjustments on account of anti-dilution or indemnification payments.

Secondary investments are made in equity shares or convertible instruments, whichever are held by the selling shareholder.

Founders generally retain continued control and are subject to lock-in requirements of instruments. The interests of the management are secured through employee stock option plans (“**ESOPs**”) or equity grants, to encourage better performance and align with the interests of the investors.

While making minority investments, private equity investors would generally ensure that the majority shareholder/founder is contractually bound along with the investee company to ensure continued performance in line with the commercial agreement. Such founders/major shareholders would be bound by transfer restrictions and minimum lock-in requirements. Investors typically negotiate robust protections such as affirmative voting rights over reserved matters, board representation, rights to secure an exit, _inter alia_, drag-along provisions, put options, or an agreed initial public offering (“**IPO**”) to enable liquidity within a defined timeline.

2.5**In relation to management equity, what is the typical range of equity allocated to the management, and what are the typical vesting and compulsory acquisition provisions?**

Generally, management equity allocations range from 5% to 15% of the share capital on a fully diluted basis, with a vesting period of three to five years. Such equity allocation is primarily influenced by factors such as sector-specific thresholds, tax benefits and compliance with regulatory requirements.

The management is contractually bound to ensure that they tender the shares during any exercise of drag right by investors or as part of an offer for sale.

While the provisions of the respective employment agreements shape the nuances of exit of key employees, typically, termination of employment emanating from circumstances beyond the employee’s control, such as death, disability, retirement, illness or superannuation, are characterised as good leavers, whereas bad leavers are those whose termination results from reasons attributable, _inter alia_, to fraud, misconduct, breach of contract, criminal implication or voluntary termination in violation of agreed terms.

3.1**What are the typical governance arrangements for private equity portfolio companies? Are such arrangements required to be made publicly available in your jurisdiction?**

The typical governance rights that are sought by private equity investors in India entail board representation, affirmative vote rights on key reserved matters and information rights.

While the transaction documents are not usually available in the public domain for investments made in private unlisted companies, such rights are typically incorporated in the by-laws, i.e. articles of association of the company, which are publicly available.

3.2**Do private equity investors and/or their director nominees typically enjoy veto rights over major corporate actions (such as acquisitions and disposals, business plans, related party transactions, etc.)? If a private equity investor takes a minority position, what veto rights would they typically enjoy?**

Yes, private equity investors and their nominee directors typically do ask for and attain affirmative vote rights with respect to major corporate actions items.

The scope of the veto matters package generally includes further equity issuance, restructuring, acquisitions, disposal of assets, related party transactions exceeding prescribed thresholds, capital expenditures and incurrence of debt exceeding prescribed thresholds, changes in senior management, material contracts, dividend, winding up of the company, liquidation, or initiation of liquidation proceedings.

3.3**Are there any limitations on the effectiveness of veto arrangements: (i) at the shareholder level; and (ii) at the director nominee level? If so, how are these typically addressed?**

Veto rights are contractual in nature and generally enforceable, with the condition that they do not violate any applicable law.

At the nominee director level, while nominee directors are appointed by the relevant investor, they owe fiduciary duties to the company on account of their directorship of the company’s board.

While veto rights offer investors significant influence, such rights should be exercised with caution for the welfare of the company and by mitigating conflict of interest.

3.4**Are there any duties owed by a private equity investor to minority shareholders such as management shareholders (or vice versa)? If so, how are these typically addressed?**

The interests of minority shareholders are protected under the Companies Act, 2013, whereby special provisions have been incorporated to deal with instances of oppression and mismanagement. The private equity investors _per se_ do not have any obligations towards other minority or management shareholders.

Generally, investors would bind the management shareholders and other minority investors under the terms of the shareholders’ agreement to ensure that they facilitate the exit.

3.5**Are there any limitations or restrictions on the contents or enforceability of shareholder agreements (including (i) governing law and jurisdiction, and (ii) non-compete and non-solicit provisions)?**

There are two basic requirements for the enforceability of shareholders’ agreements: (i) they must not be in violation of Indian laws, including exchange control laws; and (ii) the rights must not be in contravention of the articles of association adopted by the company.

As per Section 27 of the Indian Contract Act, 1892, non-compete and non-solicitation clauses are void; however, these are enforced by Indian courts on a case-to-case basis. Please note that courts generally do not agree to enforce non-compete and non-solicitation-related provisions for a long period of time.

Directors nominated by private equity investors are duty-bound to deal with actual or potential conflicts of interest, and take decisions that would benefit the company, even if it conflicts with the interests of their nominating investors. In the event of a statutory conflict, the director is required to disclose their interest and, where relevant, recuse themselves from the relevant meeting of the board. Circumstances in which conflicts arise pursuant to the involvement of directors with other portfolio companies are typically addressed through contractual arrangements and internal governance protocols to minimise risks and secure compliance.

The Companies Act, 2013 prescribe various requirements related to the appointment of directors. Further, pursuant to the requirements prescribed by the Government, security clearance is mandatory for individuals who are citizens of countries sharing a land border with India.

Directors are cast with fiduciary duties to act in good faith and may incur personal liability for breach of statutory provisions, fraud or wilful misconduct, or non-compliance. Such potential contingent liabilities are mitigated by the investors requiring the company to obtain requisite directors’ and officers’ (“**D&O**”) policy. Investors should ensure that their nominees are appointed as non-executive directors.

Any information that is available with the nominee directors with respect to the company is generally deemed to be available with the relevant nominating investor.
